page: Amazon Web Services m1.xlarge is a first-generation general-purpose server instance powered by the Xen hypervisor. It features an x86_64 architecture with 4 dedicated physical cores and 4 vCPUs, utilizing an Intel Xeon E5-2651 v2 processor running at a clock speed of 1.8 GHz. The system is equipped with 15.0 GB of system memory, yielding 3.75 GB per core. Storage is provided via 1680 GB of local HDD space, and network connectivity is rated at a baseline of 1 Gbps.

Performance benchmarks indicate that this legacy hardware delivers limited compute and memory throughput compared to modern standards. The stress-ng single-core CPU performance score of 943.8 falls into the bottom 10%, while the multi-core score of 2915.05 is in the bottom 25%. Similarly, Geekbench scores reflect lower-tier performance, with a single-core score of 496.0 and a multi-core score of 1205.0. Memory bandwidth tests show 171.47 GB/sec for cached small blocks and a lower 22.53 GB/sec for uncached large blocks, placing it in the bottom 10% to 25% range.

The primary tradeoff of the m1.xlarge is its reliance on older CPU architecture and mechanical HDD storage, which lacks the IOPS and throughput of modern SSDs. It also lacks advanced instruction sets such as AVX, AVX-512, and AMX. From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, this instance offers a high volume of local storage capacity relative to its compute tier, but its low resource density and legacy performance profile make it less efficient for modern, high-throughput workloads.

Given its hardware profile and benchmark results, the m1.xlarge is best suited for legacy applications, basic file storage, static web serving, or low-intensity database operations that require substantial local storage capacity but do not demand high CPU or memory performance.
